newsitem.title: GERMANY: German building sector wage talks collapse - union.
newsitem.headline: German building sector wage talks collapse - union.

text.p: Negotiations on 1997 wages and conditions for the some 1.3 million workers in the German construction industry broke down without conclusive agreement, officials of the IG Bau trade union said early on Saturday.

IG Bau chairman Klaus Wiesehuegel, emerging from some 14 hours of talks with employers, said an independent arbitrator would now be appointed to help find an agreement. IG Bau had entered the talks saying it wanted to ensure that wages in the industry did not fall in real terms.

A basic agreement was however reached on the key issue of bad weather payments made to construction employees when work is made impossible by poor weather, which each winter in Germany leads to sharp rises in unemployment in the sector.
Under the plan, employers will be committed to paying regular monthly wages regardless of the actual amount of time worked.
Employees will have "work-time" accounts into which any hours worked above their normal working week can be saved up to a maximum of 150 hours.
In cases of work hours lost through poor weather, the first 50 hours of lost time will be deducted from such accounts. Thereafter, the employer must assume the full cost of lost work.
After 120 hours of down-time, however, it is envisaged under the accord that the German Federal Labour Office would from then on subsidise the cost of workers' wages.
Peter Huber, chief negotiator representing the building sector employers, described the plan as a "great contribution" to reducing the steep unemployment in the industry.

The current scheme, which puts the full cost of retaining employees in times of poor weather on the employers, was widely seen as unworkable and led to many firms simply laying off much of their workforce over the winter.

No definite timescale for arbitration on the issue of 1997 wages was given by union officials or employers directly after the talks broke down. Heiner Geissler, a politican in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrat party, is expected to lead the arbitration attempt.
